Buriers
BER-ee-erz
n. pl. (men appointed to bury the dead; the burial detail after Gog)
From bury, Old English byrgan, to hide or inter. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the appointed men who went through the land after the fall of Gog, burying what the passengers marked.

Biblical Definition

And the passengers that pass through the land, when any seeth a man's bone, then shall he set up a sign by it, till the buriers have buried it in the valley of Hamongog. Ezekiel is describing the cleansing of the land after the overthrow, and he describes it as a work detail with a procedure. Seven months shall the house of Israel be burying of them, that they may cleanse the land. Men of continual employment are separated to the task; travellers who find a bone set up a marker rather than touching it; the buriers follow and inter it; the valley itself is renamed. The care is ceremonial as well as sanitary, since contact with a dead body defiled under the law, and the land itself is the thing being cleansed. What the chapter is aiming at is stated plainly at its end: I will set my glory among the heathen, and all the heathen shall see my judgment that I have executed. Scripture's honour for the dead body is rooted in the same doctrine that makes this careful: man is made in the image of God, and the body is not a discarded shell but a thing to be sown in dishonour and raised in glory.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who buries a deceased person; in Scripture, the men appointed to inter the slain of Gog and so cleanse the land.

expand to see more

BURIER, n. One who buries a deceased person.

BURY, v.t. To deposit a dead body in the earth; to inter; to entomb.

SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.

DEFILE, v.t. To make unclean; to render foul or dirty; to pollute ceremonially.

RESURRECTION, n. A rising again; the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave.

Key Scripture

Eze 39:15 — "And the passengers that pass through the land, when any seeth a man's bone, then shall he set up a sign by it, till the buriers have buried it in the valley of Hamongog."

Eze 39:12 — "And seven months shall the house of Israel be burying of them, that they may cleanse the land."

Eze 39:16 — "And also the name of the city shall be Hamonah. Thus shall they cleanse the land."

Eze 39:21 — "And I will set my glory among the heathen, and all the heathen shall see my judgment that I have executed, and my hand that I have laid upon them."

Modern Corruption

The body is treated as a husk once the person has departed, so that its disposal becomes a matter of convenience; Scripture buries with ceremony because the body is part of the man and is destined for resurrection.

expand to see more

Ezekiel gives seven months, a named valley, a corps of workers, and a marking system to the burial of enemy dead, and the trouble taken is itself a doctrine. Scripture is full of such trouble. Abraham bought a field to bury Sarah rather than accept it as a gift; Joseph made the children of Israel swear to carry his bones out of Egypt, and they did, four centuries later; Joseph of Arimathaea begged the body of Jesus and laid it in his own new tomb; devout men carried Stephen to his burial and made great lamentation over him. The body is not the discarded packaging of a soul. It is half of what a man is, and it is going to be raised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond a general carelessness, and the principle to recover is the Christian doctrine of the body. It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. That is why the church has always buried its dead with honour and hope rather than merely disposing of remains, and why the graveyard beside the meeting house was never morbid. It was a statement about what will happen there.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qabar (H6912), to bury; 'etsem (H6106), a bone; taher (H2891), to cleanse or purify.

Hebrew qabar (H6912) — to bury, to inter; till the buriers have buried it.

Hebrew 'etsem (H6106) — a bone, the substance of the body; when any seeth a man's bone.

Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, to purify; that they may cleanse the land.

Hebrew tsiyuwn (H6725) — a signpost, a marker; then shall he set up a sign by it.

Usage

"“till the buriers have buried it” — the single occurrence."

"“seven months shall the house of Israel be burying of them” — the scale of the work."

"“Thus shall they cleanse the land” — the purpose of the detail."
